Public information campaigns can help educate residents on best practices for staying safe in the dark, including safe generator use and reporting downed power lines. By taking proactive steps at both the individual and community levels, the risks associated with power outages and lack of lighting can be significantly reduced. 41 Communication Minimum Resilience Standard: Individuals have access to a communication device with connection (cellular or wifi) or have a battery-powered radio in order to receive emergency communication alerts during the full length of a power outage. Vulnerability: Everyone is vulnerable when there is a lack of communication during a power outage, as life-saving alerts may come from emergency responders. Those who are most vulnerable include individuals with caretakers they must communicate with, children, and low- income individuals who may not have access to a radio or portable batteries to charge communication devices. Potential Distributed Actions: Community members should have an emergency communication plan to utilize when they do not have access to a communication device with signal (cellular or wifi). Individuals can use battery-powered or crank radios to receive official broadcasts if they do not have access to other communication and information-sharing methods, such as social media and text messaging. Additionally, portable battery chargers are important to have on hand to keep communication devices charged. Potential Shared Solutions: Resilience Hubs can provide individuals with a place to charge their communication devices and access to information within their community through word of mouth by connecting with others who may have had more recent communication with emergency responders, other resource providers in the community, etc. Rationale: During a grid outage, maintaining effective communication is crucial for ensuring public safety, coordination, and access to critical resources. If the internet and cellular networks remain operational, community members can rely on text messages, phone calls, and social media updates to stay informed. However, even when power is out, mobile networks may still function temporarily due to backup power systems. To preserve battery life, individuals should minimize non-essential phone use, reduce screen brightness, and use text messaging rather than voice calls, as SMS requires less network capacity. Local governments and emergency organizations should prioritize sending real-time updates via social media, emergency alert systems, and local radio stations to keep residents informed. If the internet and cellular networks become unavailable, alternative communication methods become necessary. Radio remains a vital tool in such scenarios. Residents should have battery- powered or hand-crank emergency radios to receive official broadcasts from NOAA and local emergency management agencies. Individuals should prepare for outages by assembling an emergency communication plan in advance. This plan should include a list of emergency contacts, a designated family meeting place, and knowledge of local emergency radio frequencies. Keeping a written copy of important phone numbers is essential, as digital contacts may become inaccessible if devices lose power. Residents should also invest in portable power banks, solar chargers, or generator backups to extend the use of essential communication devices.
